title: POC Weekly Sync - Quantization INT8/FP8
summary: Weekly POC sync to review quantization experiments. Redwood presented INT8 and FP8 perf/quality tradeoffs on the customer's workload. INT8 shows ~25% latency reduction vs baseline with small quality regressions on rare prompts; FP8 gives additional perf gains but increases variability on hallucination-prone prompts. Agreed next steps: run 1k-prompt eval, extend bench to longer sequences, share benchmark sheet and security docs, schedule deep technical dive next week.
action_items: Alex Chen: Share updated benchmark spreadsheet (perf plots + prompt-level diffs) by 2026-12-03
Priya Nair: Run extended 1k prompt eval on FP8 with 8k sequence length and upload results by 2026-12-07
Emily Wong (BlueAtlas): Provide list of sensitive prompt categories for privacy check by 2026-12-04
Michael Torres: Validate KV-cache interaction under INT8 across 4x batch sizes and report anomalies by 2026-12-06
next_steps: Redwood to send perf + quality deck and benchmark spreadsheet
Customer to run internal acceptance on 200 priority prompts and share initial flags
Schedule technical deep-dive with BlueAtlas infra team (1h) for 2026-12-08
Exchange security artifacts: SOC2 summary + KMS integration notes
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-12-01 10:00 PST | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Nair, Michael Torres (Redwood) // Sara Gomez, Raj Patel, Emily Wong, Tom Reeves (BlueAtlas)

Auto-generated Summary: quick sync for quantization POC - int8 vs fp8 tradeoffs, runbook for next evals, and security asks.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Alex from Redwood, Priya our SE, Michael on infra. BlueAtlas team?
[00:08] Sara Gomez: Hi, Sara here, Raj, Emily, Tom on as well.
[00:12] Alex Chen: Great, outline for 45 minutes — review last week's runs, go over perf deltas, dig into any quality regressions, and decide next steps.
[00:22] Priya Nair: I'll start with the numbers we ran on your validation set of 200 prompts, note these are a mix of instructions and long-context retrieval cases. Baseline (FP16) p50 latency was ~120ms, INT8 came in at ~90ms (~25% down), and FP8 we saw p50 around 75ms. Throughput jumped roughly 1.8x for INT8 and ~2.2x for FP8 on the same instance type.
[00:46] Tom Reeves: That seems promising, what about tail latency?
[00:50] Priya Nair: tail (p95) for baseline ~420ms, INT8 ~350ms, FP8 ~380ms — FP8 improved p50 more but tail got a bit noisier, likely due to occasional kernel fallbacks. We saw a couple of outliers where the runtime switched to slower path, could be memory alignment or quant kernel jitter.
[01:15] Raj Patel: Any KV cache impact? We heavily rely on prefix caching for our RAG flows.
[01:20] Michael Torres: Good question. We instrumented KV cache hits — INT8 had equivalent cache hit rates, but the deserialization path had a small CPU overhead when converting cached KV to quantized tensors; we saw ~5-8% CPU bump in that path (we reported as KV "cash" in the logs, sorry, transcript nonsense).
[01:39] Emily Wong: From security side, any differences in exposing model internals when using FP8? Also KMS behavior unchanged?
[01:45] Alex Chen: No changes to KMS integration. All encryption at rest and transit is identical; quantization happens within the runtime after keys are applied. We'll include a short note for your security team on the isolation boundaries.
[01:58] Priya Nair: On quality — we ran automatic evals plus manual spot checks. Aggregate metric (instruction-following score) dropped by about 1.6% with INT8, and ~2.8% with FP8 on your 200 prompt validation. Most regressions were on rare tokenization cases and some multi-step reasoning prompts where small numerical drift led to different outcomes.
[02:22] Tom Reeves: Can you point to examples? That's where we worry about hallucinations.
[02:26] Priya Nair: Sure, e.g., prompt #137 — a 12-step extraction task — FP16 produced all 12 items correct, INT8 missed one item, FP8 produced a slightly different ordering and missed two. We flagged the diff in the sheet. We'll attach prompt-level diffs so you can triage.
[02:45] Sara Gomez: Do you recommend QAT or per-layer mixed quantization to reduce that?
[02:50] Priya Nair: There are a few levers: PTQ with outlier-aware calibration often fixes many cases; per-layer mixed precision (keep critical layers in FP16/32) helps a lot. QAT (quantization-aware training) is best but heavier. For POC we suggested hybrid: INT8 + selective FP16 on attention/ffn layers for risky question types.
[03:12] Raj Patel: How much complexity does hybrid add operationally? We prefer something easy to deploy.
[03:18] Michael Torres: Operationally it's a compile-time config — we ship model variants (int8, int8-mixed, fp8) as separate artifacts and runtime picks based on policy. So complexity is mostly during onboarding, not at inference. Your autoscaler and routing rules are unchanged.
[03:33] Alex Chen: Also worth calling out caching and batching recommendations we gave in the Optimize report — with quantization you can increase batch size slightly to amortize overhead, but keep an eye on latency SLO.
[03:45] Tom Reeves: Any change to token-level cost? We care about unit economics.
[03:49] Priya Nair: Per-token GPU-time is reduced; estimated cost per token down ~20-35% INT8, and ~30-45% FP8 depending on sequence length and utilization. We'll include cost examples in the spreadsheet.
[04:05] Sara Gomez: How confident are you in FP8 stability? We heard mixed from other vendors (ModelCo had some issues).
[04:12] Alex Chen: FP8 is promising but slightly less mature — more variability in kernel availability across different driver versions. We recommend starting with INT8-mixed for production and running a controlled FP8 pilot for further gains. Competitor CloudAI was mentioned as having aggressive FP8 rollout; we contrasted our approach which biases towards stability.
[04:34] Raj Patel: For our acceptance criteria, we need no more than 1.5% drop in instruction-following on 1k priority prompts and p95 latency under 500ms for common 2k-seq requests. Feasible?
[04:46] Priya Nair: Those are reasonable. Our plan: run 1k-prompt eval (your priority set) with 2 configs: INT8-mixed and FP8; capture per-prompt diffs and perf metrics. If INT8-mixed meets criteria we'll suggest ramping.
[05:02] Emily Wong: Please share the SOC2 summary and details on audit logging — we need to see retention and log schema.
[05:07] Alex Chen: Will send SOC2 one-pager + audit log export examples. Also include a short KMS integration note.
[05:15] Tom Reeves: On bench infra — what instance types did you use? Ours are similar to G5-like, we want reproducibility.
[05:21] Michael Torres: We used GPU A100x2 equivalent for this run (config attached in sheet). We can re-run on G5-equivalent; it mostly affects perf numbers but relative deltas hold. We'll mark instance type per run.
[05:34] Priya Nair: Quick note on observed anomalies: a handful of prompts triggered tokenization differences where byte-level rounding in FP8 changed punctuation handling. We're working on tokenizer-preserving calibration to reduce that.
[05:49] Sara Gomez: Is there any risk to data residency or retention when you run these evals? We prefer to run the 1k eval within our VPC.
[05:56] Alex Chen: Totally fine — for the POC we can run the bench inside your Dedicated or private deployment, or we can send a sanitized run result. We'll coordinate with Raj on access.
[06:06] Priya Nair: Proposed timeline: bench run this week (Priya/Michael do the FP8 + INT8-mixed), customer provides 1k prompt set by end of week, results back early next week.
[06:17] Raj Patel: I'll get the prompt set ready and confirm VPC access.
[06:20] Alex Chen: Cool. Anything else on quality?
[06:23] Tom Reeves: Curious about calibration runtime costs — how long does PTQ calibration take for 1k prompts?
[06:28] Priya Nair: Typically a few minutes per model on a single GPU for off-line calibration, depends on sample size. We'll include wall-clock numbers.
[06:35] Sara Gomez: For the deep-dive next week can we include someone from our infra team to look at autoscaling interplay?
[06:40] Alex Chen: Absolutely — we'll set a 60-minute slot and include our infra lead.
[06:44] Priya Nair: I'll also prepare a short written note on mitigation patterns: per-layer mix, outlier clipping, tokenizer-preserving calibrators, and fallback routing to FP16 for flagged prompts.
[06:58] Michael Torres: On routing: we can implement a policy that routes flagged prompt types to FP16/INT8-mixed automatically with header-based tags. That avoids broad rollback.
[07:10] Raj Patel: That would be ideal. Keep rollback automated.
[07:14] Alex Chen: Ok, recap and owners. We'll send the benchmark spreadsheet link (shared drive) and the perf deck. Priya will run the extended FP8 run and Michael will validate KV cache behavior. BlueAtlas to share prompt set and security contacts.
[07:28] Tom Reeves: One small ask — can you include prompt-level diffs exported as CSV so we can ingest into our triage tracker?
[07:34] Priya Nair: Yes, CSV + diff highlights.
[07:38] Emily Wong: Also include redaction notes in the sheet if any prompts contain PII.
[07:42] Alex Chen: Noted.
[07:44] Sara Gomez: Thanks all. Good progress.
[07:47] Alex Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with artifacts and schedule the deep-dive for Tue 12/08.
[07:53] Meeting end.

Notes / Links mentioned: benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example/reports/blueatlas-quant-bench-2026-12-01), perf deck, SOC2 one-pager, KMS integration note, quantization whitepaper (Redwood internal).

Quality / Transcript caveats: automated transcription had some mis-attributions and occasional "KV cash" instead of KV cache; speaker overlap truncated in a couple places.
